summary: [FAIL] One blocking issue found in cli.py: the run_queue.register() call is unguarded — an OSError from non-blocking lock contention (filelock.py uses LK_NBLCK / LOCK_NB) propagates through _run() uncaught and crashes the orchestrator process with an unhandled exception when two concurrent runs start simultaneously on the same workspace. unregister() is correctly guarded with try/except in the finally block; register() must be guarded symmetrically. run_queue.py and test_run_queue.py are high quality — architecture, locking, atomic write, and tests all reviewed and approved. Only cli.py integration needs rework.

comments.note: BLOCKING — cli.py line ~574: run_queue.register() is unguarded against OSError. filelock.py's lock_exclusive() uses non-blocking mode (LOCK_NB / LK_NBLCK), which raises OSError immediately if the queue lock is held by another process. If two orchestrators start concurrently on the same workspace (different plans), one will raise OSError inside register(), which propagates through _run() (no except clause on the outer try, only a finally), exits asyncio.run(), and is not caught by main()'s `except KeyboardInterrupt` — resulting in an unhandled exception crash. Fix: wrap the register() call in try/except, log a warning on failure, and allow the run to continue with entry_id = None. The unregister() call in the finally block is already correctly guarded — register() must match this pattern.

run_queue.py: _LOCK_FILE.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) on line ~86 is a no-op since _LOGS_DIR.mkdir() immediately above creates the same directory. Harmless dead code. Recommend removing it during rework to eliminate confusion for future readers. (Also flagged by QA.)

run_queue.py: The locking pattern (os.open + lock_exclusive + unlock + os.close) is internally consistent with filelock.py, but diverges from the pattern used in cli.py (open(lock_path, 'w') + fileno()). Both are correct and cross-platform, but the inconsistency is worth noting. No action required; documenting for awareness.

comments.note: cli.py register() guard: log.warning() does not pass exc_info=True. If a non-OSError exception is raised (e.g., an ImportError from a broken import, or a UUID-generation edge case), the cause is swallowed silently. Adding exc_info=True to the warning would aid future debugging at zero cost. Not blocking — the guard is correct as-is.

cli.py unregister() guard in finally: uses bare `except Exception: pass` with no log statement. An asymmetry exists: register() failure is logged, unregister() failure is silent. A stale queue entry (from unregister failing) is more user-visible than a missing registration, so surfacing the failure at DEBUG level would improve observability. Low priority — not blocking.
